title: How Silly Putty Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the history and science of Silly Putty. They trace the rubber backdrop (Charles Goodyear's vulcanization, the Amazon rubber boom, British seedling hybrids in Southeast Asia, and WWII synthetic rubber development including GR-S). They describe James Wright's GE "bouncing putty," Peter Hodgson's 1950 marketing via Block toy store, Neiman Marcus and Doubleday bookshops, and the New Yorker article that spurred sales. The episode covers the putty's non-Newtonian, viscoelastic behavior and viscosity, a listener email (Matthew, age eleven) explaining non-Newtonian fluids, a homemade recipe using glue, water and borax, and a listener email from Josephine on the dumbing down of culture and the Internet.
topics: New Yorker Talk of the Town

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck banter about their shirts, hats and beards before starting the show.

segments.title: Vulcanization and Charles Goodyear
segments.summary: Charles Goodyear's 1839 vulcanization process made natural rubber tougher and more flexible, enabling mass-produced tires, hoses and belts during the Industrial Revolution.

segments.title: Rubber boom and Southeast Asian plantations
segments.summary: The Amazon rubber boom enriched Brazil until 1876, when British men smuggled seeds to London's botanical gardens and developed hybrids grown in British Southeast Asian colonies, which later overtook Brazil's dominance by 1920.

segments.title: WWII rubber shortage and synthetic rubber
segments.summary: Japan's invasion of Southeast Asia cut the US rubber supply, and the War Production Board drove development of synthetic rubber, leading to GR-S (Government Rubber Styrene).

segments.title: James Wright's bouncing putty and Peter Hodgson
segments.summary: GE chemist James Wright created a failed synthetic rubber, a bouncing putty made from boric acid and silicone oil. Peter Hodgson, a New Haven ad agency owner, saw it at a cocktail party and sold it through the Block toy store catalog for two dollars.

segments.title: Manufacturing, naming and the New Yorker boom
segments.summary: Hodgson borrowed money, bought a batch from GE, packaged putty in plastic eggs, sold it at Doubleday and Neiman Marcus, and opened a Connecticut plant. A 1950 New Yorker Talk of the Town piece about Doubleday sales led to a quarter million orders in three days. Hodgson died in 1976, with sales in 22 countries.
topics: New Yorker Talk of the Town

segments.title: Kids, adult intent and uses
segments.summary: Hodgson intended Silly Putty for adults to relieve stress, but kids bought it in large numbers. Kids used it to copy comics and newsprint. Non-toxicity meant mouthing it caused no harm.

segments.title: Science: viscosity and non-Newtonian fluids
segments.summary: Silly Putty is a viscoelastic polymer, a fluid whose behavior depends on flow time, temperature and force. Viscosity measures resistance to flow, measured in pascal seconds or poise. Newtonian fluids like water have constant viscosity, while non-Newtonian fluids change with applied stress.

segments.title: Listener mail: non-Newtonian fluids from Matthew
segments.summary: Eleven-year-old listener Matthew explains Newtonian and non-Newtonian fluids, using cornstarch and water (oobleck) as an example. The hosts discuss the email and mention a super ball comparison.

segments.title: Homemade Silly Putty recipe
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh describe making Silly Putty at home with white glue, warm water, food coloring and borax, explaining how borax cross-links the polymer chains.

segments.title: Listener mail: smart stuff from Josephine
segments.summary: Josephine from Columbia, South Carolina writes about the dumbing down of culture and the Internet, arguing that the Internet supports research and connections. Hosts also issue a cheddar cheese correction.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close the episode and point listeners to the website and social media for more on Silly Putty.
